messages.subject: Results
parts:
Dear team,

First, I would like to thank you for setting up this group.

I have been working on a dataset about Common Waxbill and I have some doubts I would like to share with you. We made 23 visits/surveys (point counts of 80 m radius) in two different wetlands (37 points in one and 34 points in the other).  In total, 152 detections of 486 birds. My hypothesis is to estimate the population in relation to three different possible covariates:

Study.Area: The surveys were carried out by two ornithologists, each one only surveyed one of the two habitats/wetlands. So the study area also includes the effect of the observer.

Habitat: the habitat where surveys were carried out is a mosaic of reeds, paddy fields, orchards, etc.

Size group: Waxbills tend to fly in flocks during Autumn, Winter, and early spring, so I was testing any size effect in detection.

 The data are sparse, I think because of the difficulties of detecting the species (very vocal but small species) in a dense vegetation habitat (reeds, orange plantations, etc), so I have to apply truncation="45"

The two best models (AIC) are hazard rate including Study Area, and the second one including Study Area and Size. Both P-values of CV(Cramér–von Mises tests ) are above 0.05, however, the estimated detection probability is low. I am attaching the model selections, GOF test, and the detection probability of the best model. 


I would appreciate any suggestions about the results and analysis.

Many thanks

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Results
parts:
Pau

Thank you for the compliment.

From your description of the survey, it seems possible that the "study area" effect and the "habitat" effect are partially confounded. Were different "habitats" recorded in one "study area"?

You mention that you used point counts with 80m truncation in the field. You may have been caught out by using the argument truncation="45"​ in your call to the ds​ function. Because of the quotes, the software interprets this as a percentage; hence the truncation distance shown in the detection function figure you attached was truncated at ~25m not 45m. I don't know which you intended.

I concur that the two models with the smallest AIC both fit your data (according to the CvM test). There seems to be virtually no influence of group size upon detectability; the model with size alone finishes last and the deltaAIC value between the top two models is quite small.

However, your detection function plot is quite telling. It appears that in one "study area" detectability falls off quite rapidly, whereas in the other "study area" detectability is perfect to the edge of the plot (~25m). Is it biologically plausible that detectability differs that radically between the "study areas", or is that pattern the result of small sample size?

One final point to mention, not just for your analysis, but for others reading this exchange. Note the outrageous se(detection probability) for some of the models (three covariate model, habitat alone, habitat+size). Those standard errors are symptomatic of something gone wrong with the model fitting, those results are not reliable and the models should not be used for inference.
